title: 2B Reversal
teaches: The 2B bottom as we trade it: a stock breaks a prior swing low for the first time, goes no more than 3% under it and fails to follow through; the buy is a market order only after price trades back above the broken low, within 3 sessions, no more than 4% above it; the stop sits a few cents under the lowest low of the undercut, a close back under the broken low is a warning, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and a market still making lower lows is not the place.

walkthroughs.title: QCOM, September 2020: the same-day reclaim
steps: QCOM, September 2020. The September 8 low, 109.62, is nine sessions old. Price drifts back to it and everyone's watching.
September 21, the last bar, it undercuts that low by 1.20%. The sellers can't follow through. It's back above the same session.
That reclaim is the trigger. Buy at market, 109.63. Stop 108.25, a few cents under the day's low, 1.26% away.
Back under the low, you're out. It hit 3R next day. Move the stop to breakeven and let it work.

walkthroughs.title: PYPL, March 2018: a fill at the open, and a loss
steps: March 2, 2018: PYPL sets a low at 76.93. It holds three weeks, then gets undercut by 0.75%, closing under it.
Next day, March 26, it opens back over the low at 77.98, 1.4% above it. Your market order fills at the open.
Only 1.4% over, inside our 4% limit, so it's buyable. Stop 76.30 under the undercut low, 2.15% away.
Next day it falls through the stop, with SPY still making lower lows. Small, planned loss. The stop did its job.

questions.q: You'll hear traders talk about the 2B all the time. Whose idea was it?
choices: Victor Sperandeo
Larry Williams
Thomas Bulkowski
Linda Raschke
questions.why: Victor Sperandeo. He laid it out in his book, Trader Vic, Methods of a Wall Street Master. The idea is simple. A stock breaks an old high or low, then can't carry through. That failure is the signal. Whoever sold the break is now on the wrong side. Bulkowski wrote the pattern up on his site later, and he credits Sperandeo.
questions.lesson_line: The 2B is Sperandeo's. A break that fails is the signal.

wrong.Larry Williams: Not his. Bulkowski's page names Sperandeo as the source.
wrong.Linda Raschke: Not hers. The 2B is Sperandeo's, from Trader Vic.
wrong.Thomas Bulkowski: He wrote the pattern up on his site, but he credits Sperandeo with it.

questions.q: Last bar: the first trade under its March low, about 1.8% under it, then a close back above it the same day. That's a 2B.
questions.why: True. That's the 2B. It's the first time price trades under that 483.65 low. It only gets 1.8% under, and the sellers can't follow through. By the close it's back above. questions.lesson_line: No reclaim, no trade. Buying the undercut is guessing.
questions.simple: False. Buying the break is guessing, so we wait until price trades back above the broken low.

questions.q: Your stock is slicing under an old swing low right now, and it keeps going. Why do you care how deep it gets?
choices: Your stop goes under that low
Deeper traps more sellers
It sets your profit target
It doesn't, only the reclaim counts
questions.answer: Your stop goes under that low
questions.why: Because your stop goes a few cents under the lowest low of the undercut. However deep it slips, that's how far your stop sits from your buy. A shallow undercut, about 3% or less, keeps the stop in the 1 to 3% I like. Let it slide a lot deeper and the stop slides with it. How deep is too deep is a judgment call. But a deep undercut at full size is how a small loss gets big. If it goes deeper, buy fewer shares or wait for a tighter entry.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow undercut, close stop. Deep undercut, wide stop.

wrong.Deeper traps more sellers: Maybe, but you pay for it. The stop sits under that low, so deeper means wider risk.
wrong.It sets your profit target: Targets come from your R and the push. The depth sets your stop.
wrong.It doesn't, only the reclaim counts: The reclaim is the trigger. The depth still decides where your stop goes.

questions.simple: Your stop goes under the undercut low. The deeper it slips, the wider your stop and the fewer shares you can buy.

deeper.counter: DELL, 2024-07-22: it closed back above its 127.59 low, but only after going 4.36% under it. The stop that followed was 4.83% from the entry. The reclaim doesn't fix a deep undercut.

reasons: +2 rests on the rulebook's stop line (A13) and the card's 3% depth

questions.lesson_line: Judge the reclaim by the close, not the open.
questions.simple: False, a reclaim day that closes near its low means the buyers gave up. We want a close in the upper half.

deeper.trap: The trap is counting any trade back above the low as a reclaim. The close decides it: the upper half of the day's range, or it's not a trigger.

questions.lesson_line: Three sessions to reclaim. After that it is a breakdown.
questions.simple: 3. With no close back above the broken low within 3 sessions, it is a breakdown, not a 2B.

It paid here, but the rule is about odds over many trades, not one chart.

questions.q: How would you describe this setup to a friend, in one line?
choices: A failed first break of a swing low
A gap down that reclaims the prior close
A 2 ATR flush on 2x volume at a low
A dip under a rising 50-day, then back
questions.answer: A failed first break of a swing low
questions.why: A failed first break of a swing low. It breaks under an old low for the first time, gets no more than 3% under, and can't follow through. Then it's back above. The other three look close, but they're different setups. A gap down that takes back yesterday's close is an Oops. A flush of 2 ATR on 2x volume is a capitulation. A dip under a rising 50-day is a U&R. MU did the 2B on 2024-02-20, 1.77% under its 80.58 low and back above.
questions.lesson_line: A 2B is a failed break of a swing low. Name the level first.

wrong.A gap down that reclaims the prior close: That's the Oops. It's judged on yesterday's low, not an old swing low.
wrong.A 2 ATR flush on 2x volume at a low: That's a capitulation, a hard flush. A 2B is a shallow slip under an old low.
wrong.A dip under a rising 50-day, then back: When the level is a rising average, it's a U&R. A 2B needs a swing low.

questions.simple: A 2B is the first break of an old swing low that fails fast and gets back above it.

deeper.trap: The shape looks the same, so name the level first. A swing low at least 5 sessions old is a 2B. Yesterday's low is an Oops. A rising 20 EMA or 50-day, a prior high, a round number or the 10-session range low is a U&R.

reasons: +2 the look-alike tells are the card's proposed criteria

questions.story: Last bar: it dipped under a swing low from early January for the first time, then closed back above it.

questions.q: Bulkowski on the 2B: it gets you into a double bottom sooner, but the risk of a failed trade is much greater.

That's fine, as long as you trade it that way. Small, defined risk, a real stop with your broker, and when it hits you're out. A faster entry isn't a safer one.
questions.lesson_line: Earlier in means more misses. The stop keeps them small.
questions.simple: True, the 2B gets you in before a double bottom confirms. More of those trades fail, so keep the stop tight.

reasons: +2 the claim is attributed to Bulkowski's page, which is the only publisher

questions.q: You're scanning for 2Bs. Where do you most want that undercut low to sit?

Far from any moving average
Far under the 200-day
Right after a big red news bar
questions.why: Right at the 50-day or the 200-day. Then you've got two reasons for buyers to show up at the same spot, the old low and a big average. That's what I want to see. It's a plus, not a must, so a clean 2B away from the averages still counts. The ones to skip are under the 200-day, where we don't buy stocks. And ones that broke on a big red news candle.
questions.lesson_line: An old low sitting on a big average. That's the spot.

wrong.Far under the 200-day: Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line.
wrong.Far from any moving average: It can still count, but it's not the best spot. We like the low right on the 50-day or 200-day.
wrong.Right after a big red news bar: We want an orderly drift into the low. A big red news candle right before the break is a different story.

questions.simple: Right on the 50-day or the 200-day. The old low and a big average give buyers two reasons to step in.

reasons: +2 'best when' is the card's proposed preference, not a rulebook line

So you're out at once, and the stop order with your broker does it for you. Don't wait for a close to see if it comes back. MGM tagged the 30.26 stop to the cent the next day, and twenty sessions later it was 31.98. That stings. The stop still did its job.
questions.lesson_line: Under the new low, you're out. No waiting, no hoping.
questions.simple: True, once price trades under the new low the 2B failed. You're out, no waiting for the close.

Half
All of it
A quarter

RL got there on day 1, and we very rarely sell on day 1.

It reclaims later the same day
It reclaims on the very next day
It undercuts by 1% and reclaims

wrong.It undercuts by 1% and reclaims: A shallow undercut is what we want.
wrong.It reclaims on the very next day: A reclaim in a day or two is inside the window.

questions.simple: Six closes under the low is too long for a 2B, which must close back above within 3 sessions.

deeper.trap: Counting is the whole test. A close back above within 3 sessions is a 2B. Five or more closes under, then a retake of the line, is a Remount. GS on 2017-01-25 had 6 closes under the 236.64 low before the first close back above.

reasons: +2 keyed on the card's proposed 3-session window while the reclaim-window grading is held (D-102)
+1 a count that sits near the edge (4 closes fits neither label cleanly)

questions.q: The reclaim looks clean. Do you take it?
choices: No, earnings are 3 sessions out
Yes, the chart's all that matters
No, 2Bs don't work near reports
Yes, then sell before the report
questions.story: Here's the day before. Tomorrow it undercuts its swing low and takes it back the same session. Earnings come 3 sessions after that.
questions.why: No. We don't make a new buy in the 3 sessions before a report. A report can gap a stock right through your stop overnight, and you take a much bigger loss than you planned. AAPL is the painful example. It took back its low on 2014-10-15 and was up 14.1% twenty sessions later. Still not a buy, because the report came 2014-10-20. If you're already in and up 5R, you can hold through. A new buy, no.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 sessions before a report.

wrong.Yes, then sell before the report: That's still a new buy inside the window. We don't make it.
wrong.Yes, the chart's all that matters: The report is its own risk. A gap can jump right over your stop.
wrong.No, 2Bs don't work near reports: Right call, wrong reason. The rule is no new buys in the 3 sessions before a report.

questions.simple: No. Earnings are too close, and a report can gap right past your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B22 (settled)

questions.q: Clean chart, tight stop. What's the play?
choices: Pass, the market's still falling
Take it at full size on the reclaim
Take it, the leader is strong
Pass, the undercut was too deep
questions.story: A leader undercuts its low by 0.75% and takes it back the same day. The trigger is 83.03, stop 82.35. The market and the chip group are still making lower lows.
questions.why: Pass for now. The chart's fine, the market isn't. The best 2Bs come as the indexes wash out under their own lows and take them back. Here they're still making lower lows, with no reclaim. One stock can't carry a falling market. NVDA's next day opened 83.15 and fell to 75.61, a 10% day straight through the stop. Keep it on your radar and wait for the market to turn.
questions.lesson_line: A clean 2B in a falling market is still a falling market.

wrong.Take it at full size on the reclaim: Size doesn't fix it. The market's the problem, not the chart.
wrong.Take it, the leader is strong: Strong on its own didn't save NVDA or AMD that week. The market won.
wrong.Pass, the undercut was too deep: Right call, wrong reason. 0.75% is shallow. The market's the problem.

questions.simple: Pass, the chart is clean but the market is still falling. Wait for it to turn.

reasons: +2 the market gate is the card's proposed criterion

questions.q: That close stings. What do you do with the position?
choices: Hold to the stop, don't add
Sell at the close to be safe
Add on the dip to lower the cost
Lower the stop to give it room
questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 100.05, stop 98.70. Next day it closes 99.40, back under the 100.00 low but above your stop.
questions.answer: Hold to the stop, don't add
questions.why: Hold to the stop and don't add. A close back under the broken low within 2 sessions is a warning. The failure might be failing. But your stop's at 98.70 and it hasn't traded there. The stop is your exit, not a bad feeling at the close. What you don't do is add. Adding to a trade that's flashing a warning is how a small loss gets big.
questions.lesson_line: A close back under the low is a warning. Let the stop do its job.

wrong.Sell at the close to be safe: The stop is the exit. Selling on a scary close is trading on feel.
wrong.Add on the dip to lower the cost: Never add after a warning. That turns a small loss into a big one.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: Stops only move up. Lowering it just makes the loss bigger if it fails.

questions.simple: Hold to your stop and don't add. A close back under the low is a warning, not your exit.

deeper.example: TSLA, 2023-08-11: bought at 240.71, stop 237.97. The next session opened 235.70, under the level, and it fell to 212.36 by 08-18. The failure failed.

reasons: rests on the card's warning rule and the owner's rulebook A4

questions.q: You got stopped by a penny. What now?
choices: Take it, wait for a new trigger
Buy back now with the same stop
Buy back now with a wider stop
Drop this stock from your list
questions.story: You bought at 30.83, stop 30.26. The next day's low tags 30.26 to the cent and you're out. Now it's bouncing.
questions.answer: Take it, wait for a new trigger
questions.why: Take the loss and wait for a new trigger. The stop did its job, even if a penny stings. To get back in you need a new reason, a fresh trigger with its own stop and every rule. Jumping back in because it bounced is a revenge trade. MGM hit the stop to the cent and was 31.98 twenty sessions later. That's trading. If it sets up again, you take it fresh.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is the plan working. Come back only on a new trigger.

wrong.Buy back now with the same stop: That's the same trade with no new trigger. A new try needs a new setup.
wrong.Buy back now with a wider stop: Widening to stay in is how small losses turn big. New trigger, new stop.
wrong.Drop this stock from your list: No need. The stop did its job. If it sets up again, it's a new trade.

questions.simple: Take the loss. The stop did its job, and a new try needs a new trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B21 (settled)

questions.q: Your stop got jumped. What's the call?
choices: Out now, the loss is past 2R
Hold, the new stop is 96.40
Keep the stop at 98.70 and wait
Buy more at 96.40 to lower your cost
questions.story: You bought at 100.05, stop 98.70, so 1.35 a share at risk. Overnight news hits. It gaps open at 97.00 and the first 30-minute low is 96.40.
questions.answer: Out now, the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Out now. On a gap through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide. Normally that 30-minute low becomes your new stop. But there's a ceiling. From 100.05 down to 96.40 is more than twice your 1.35 of risk, so you're past 2R. Past 2R, you just get out. Don't let one gap turn into the trade that wrecks your month.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: the first 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Hold, the new stop is 96.40: That only works while the loss is inside 2R. Here it's past it.
wrong.Keep the stop at 98.70 and wait: That stop's already been jumped. It can't protect you now.
wrong.Buy more at 96.40 to lower your cost: Never add to a loser. The rule says get out.

questions.simple: Out now. The first 30-minute low would cost you more than 2R, so there's no new stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the first 30-minute low as the new stop every time. It's the new stop only while the loss stays inside 2R. Here the drop from 100.05 to 96.40 is more than twice your 1.35 of risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B20 and its 2R ceiling

questions.q: Fill 50.01 and stop 48.75. How far is the stop from the fill, in percent?
questions.why: 2.5%. Inside the usual 3% line, so the stop fits at full size.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stop against 3% before you size.

questions.q: It's working. Where does 5R sit on your chart?
questions.why: $45.49. Your R is the fill minus the stop, 42.89 minus 42.37. Five of those on top of the 42.89 fill lands at 45.49. I care about 5R because selling into a push, somewhere around 5 to 10R, is often where the first sell goes. It's still a judgment, not an order. Mark it and let the stock show you.
questions.lesson_line: Know 3R and 5R before the open. Then let the stock show you.
questions.simple: 45.49. One R is the fill minus the stop, and 5R adds five of those to the fill.

reasons: a computed key

wrong.$40.29: You took 5R off the fill. That's under your stop.
wrong.$44.97: You built it off the stop. Start from the fill.
wrong.$46.01: That's six R, one too many.

questions.story: You bought 42.89 as it took back the broken low. Stop 42.37, a few cents under the undercut.

questions.q: Up 3R on day 1. What do you do?
choices: Hold it all, no sell this early
Sell a third, stop to breakeven
Sell it all and take the win
Sell half, keep the original stop
questions.story: You bought 49.58, stop 49.15. The very next session it rips to 3R.
questions.answer: Hold it all, no sell this early
questions.why: Hold it all. I almost never sell on day 1. Day 3 at the earliest, and I'm looking for a 3, 5 or 7 day push to sell into. A move this fast is the stock showing you it wants to go. Don't cut a fresh winner on its first pop. RL hit 3R on day 1 and kept going. Your stop's still there if it turns.
questions.lesson_line: 3R on day 1 isn't a sell signal. Let it push.

wrong.Sell it all and take the win: You'd cut a fresh winner on its first pop. We give it days.
wrong.Sell half, keep the original stop: Still selling on day 1. We almost never do.
wrong.Sell a third, stop to breakeven: A third at 3R isn't how we sell. Day 1 is too early.

questions.simple: Hold it all. Day 1 is too early to sell, so wait for a push of a few days.

deeper.example: RL on 2009-07-08 was bought at 49.58, stop 49.15, and hit 3R on day 1. We very rarely sell on day 1, and we wait until day 3 at the earliest.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
+1 the trim levels are marked adjustable

questions.q: Nothing's wrong, but nothing's happening. What do you do?
choices: Sell it and free the money
Hold on, aiming for 5R
Add if it breaks out higher
Widen the stop to give it room
questions.story: It's been 10 trading days since you bought this 2B. It's chopped sideways and sits at +0.7R. The stop's never been touched.
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. Ten trading days and still under 1R means the idea didn't work, even though the stop never hit. Meanwhile your money's tied up in a stock doing nothing, and you're missing the ones that are moving. Sell it, free the cash, and put it in a better setup. If it sets up again, you can buy it back on a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R: sell it and move on.

wrong.Hold on, aiming for 5R: Hoping for 5R isn't a plan. Under 1R after 10 days, you sell.
wrong.Add if it breaks out higher: Adding to a stalled trade makes no sense. The time stop sells it.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: A stop never moves wider. And room isn't the problem, time is.

questions.simple: Sell it. A trade stuck under 1R for 10 days is tying up money you could use better.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Everything's firing at once. How many do you buy?
choices: A few, add as they work
A few now, the rest tomorrow
All eight now, at full size
All eight now, at half size
questions.story: The market filter in our app just flipped back to Green, our all-clear, after a correction. Eight 2Bs take back their lows in one morning.
questions.answer: A few, add as they work
questions.why: A few, and add as they work. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all eight, it fails, and eight stops hit at once. Start with a few of the best. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add more. If they fail, you lost a little and you're still mostly in cash. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: Back from a correction, start with a few. Let the market earn your exposure.

wrong.All eight now, at full size: If the turn's a fake, eight stops hit at once.
wrong.All eight now, at half size: Half size on eight is still eight bets on one market call. Start with a few.
wrong.A few now, the rest tomorrow: A date isn't a reason. Add when the first ones work, not on a schedule.

questions.simple: A few, then add as they work. If the turn is fake, you only lose a little.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading Green as all in. Green allows full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. But right after a correction we start with a few, and open more only as the first ones work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F68 (settled)
fixed before

questions.q: When do you take your 3R trim?
choices: At the start of trading
At that day's close
On a fall to 62.40
Wait until it hits 5R
questions.story: Your 3R level is 62.40. The next morning the stock opens at 63.10.
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The 3R level was 62.40 and the open, 63.10, is already past it. Do not wait for a fall back to 62.40, and do not wait for 5R: the hard rule takes the first trim at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Open past the level, take the trim at the open.

wrong.At that day's close: The rule is to take the trim at the open.
wrong.On a fall to 62.40: The rule is to take it at the open, not to wait for a fall back.
wrong.Wait until it hits 5R: The hard rule takes the first trim at 3R. The open is past it.

questions.simple: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook F63 (settled)

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a steadier name?
choices: The 20 EMA
The 50-day
The 200-day
The 5-day
questions.why: The 20 EMA. Sell on a close below it. Fast movers trail the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Steadier name, 20 EMA. Fast mover, 9 EMA. Sell on a close below.

wrong.The 50-day: Too slow for the default trail.
wrong.The 200-day: That is the long-term line, far too slow for a trail.
wrong.The 5-day: The defaults are the 9 EMA and the 20 EMA.

questions.q: How do you play it?
choices: Take it only if it grades A+
Take it at full size, as in Green
Take it smaller, as in Yellow
Pass, only Green allows it
questions.story: A clean 2B reclaims its low, but the market reading is Orange.
questions.answer: Take it only if it grades A+
questions.why: Take it only as an A+. In an Orange market only A+ setups are allowed.
questions.lesson_line: Orange market, A+ only. Yellow, smaller. Green, full.

wrong.Pass, only Green allows it: Orange allows an A+, so Green is not the only reading that does.
wrong.Take it smaller, as in Yellow: Smaller and fewer is the Yellow reading. Orange is A+ only.

questions.simple: In an Orange market only the best setups are allowed, so take it only if it grades A+.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, the market reading guide)
+1 the reading is a guide, not a fixed table

questions.q: Great chart, Red market. How do you play it?
choices: Mostly cash, plus shorts
Full risk, up to 10 positions
Smaller and fewer positions
Only A+ setups are allowed
questions.story: A clean 2B takes back its low today. Our market filter, the app's Green to Red reading of the market, says Red.
questions.why: Mostly cash. Red means the market's in real trouble, and good-looking setups fail more often when the market's against them. A clean 2B doesn't change that. The reading is a guide, not a law, but in Red I'm mostly sitting on my hands. The other side of the guide is shorts below the 200-day. Put this one on your radar. When the filter turns back to Green, start with a few and add as they work.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, mostly cash. Keep the good charts on your radar.

wrong.Full risk, up to 10 positions: That's Green. Red is the other end of the scale.
wrong.Smaller and fewer positions: That's Yellow. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Only A+ setups are allowed: That's Orange. In Red you're mostly in cash.

questions.simple: Mostly cash. A clean chart doesn't beat a bad market, so keep it on your radar and wait.

deeper.counter: A clean shape doesn't change the market reading. In Red the guide is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. When the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add only as the first ones work.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, D46)

questions.q: Sperandeo says an intermediate 2B usually turns within three to five weeks of the new low.
questions.why: False. Days, not weeks. His line is that the new high or low usually breaks within three to five days. A real 2B turns fast. That's how we trade it too. If it's still stuck under the broken low a week later, it's not a failed break anymore. It's a breakdown, and you leave it alone.
questions.lesson_line: A 2B turns in days, not weeks.
questions.simple: False, Sperandeo says three to five days, not weeks. A real 2B turns fast.

deeper.counter: Sperandeo gives three to five days for an intermediate 2B. We want the close back above the broken low fast, about 3 sessions as a guide. Both count in days.

reasons: one web quote carries the key
the card's 3-session count is proposed
fixed before

questions.q: Your 2B is up 6R and earnings come out tomorrow night. You're allowed to hold it through the report.
questions.why: True. Up 5R or more, you can hold through. A report can gap a stock hard either way, right past any stop. That's why we want the 5R cushion first, so a bad gap eats profit and not your account. Under 5R, you're out before the report. And no new buys in the 3 days before one.
questions.lesson_line: Hold through a report only with a 5R cushion.
questions.simple: True. Past 5R you have a cushion for a bad gap, so you can hold through the report.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Yesterday's low got taken out and taken back. What are you looking at?
choices: An Oops, the low is one day old
A 2B, it reclaimed on the same day
A breakdown, it broke a low
A spring, it closed back inside
questions.story: Yesterday closed at 83.20 with a low of 82.40. Today opens at 82.70, trades down to 82.10 and closes at 83.60.
questions.answer: An Oops, the low is one day old
questions.why: An Oops. Walk through it. It opened 82.70, under yesterday's 83.20 close. It broke yesterday's 82.40 low, then closed 83.60, back over that close. That's the Oops: a gap down that takes back the prior close. A 2B needs a swing low at least 5 sessions old, and this low is one day old. Check the age of the low before you name it.
questions.lesson_line: Check the age of the low. One day old is an Oops.

wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed on the same day: Same-day is fine for a 2B, but the low has to be 5 sessions old. This one's from yesterday.
wrong.A breakdown, it broke a low: It closed back above. A breakdown stays under.
wrong.A spring, it closed back inside: A spring's level is the floor of a range of 15 sessions or more. This was yesterday's low.

questions.simple: An Oops. It broke yesterday's low and took back the prior close, and a 2B needs an older low.

deeper.trap: The shape looks like a 2B, so check the age of the low and the open. An Oops opens under the prior close and breaks yesterday's low. A 2B breaks a swing low at least 5 sessions old. Calling every dip under yesterday's low a 2B is the mistake.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed look-alike tell (Oops)

questions.q: What do you call this one?
choices: A 2B, it broke an old swing low
An Oops, it retook a prior close
A Remount, it reclaimed late
A spring, it closed back inside
questions.story: Last bar: it broke a swing low from twelve sessions back and closed under it. Tomorrow it closes back above.
questions.answer: A 2B, it broke an old swing low
questions.why: A 2B. Two checks: the age of the low and the time spent under it. The low is twelve sessions old, past the 5 a 2B needs. It closes under once, then gets back above, well inside 3 sessions. An Oops would be yesterday's low, taken back the same day. A Remount would sit under the line for five closes or more. DINO took back its 42.88 low on 2018-03-01 and hit 3R on day 2.
questions.lesson_line: An older swing low and a reclaim in a day or two. That's a 2B.

wrong.An Oops, it retook a prior close: An Oops breaks yesterday's low and takes back the prior close the same day. This low is twelve sessions old.
wrong.A Remount, it reclaimed late: A Remount comes after five or more closes under the level. This had one.
wrong.A spring, it closed back inside: A spring's level is the floor of a range of 15 sessions or more, not a single swing low.

questions.simple: A 2B. The low it broke was twelve sessions old, and it got back above the next day.

deeper.trap: Two tests split the look-alikes: how old the broken low is, and how many closes under before the reclaim. Twelve sessions old and back above the next day passes both.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed look-alike tells (Oops, Remount)

questions.q: Same-day dip and reclaim. Which setup is it?
choices: A 2B, it's an older low
An Oops, reclaimed the same day
A Remount, it retook an old low
A breakdown, it broke a low
questions.story: Here's the day before. Tomorrow it opens above a swing low from thirteen sessions back, dips under it, and closes back above.
questions.why: A 2B. Same-day doesn't make it an Oops. The level does: an Oops is yesterday's low and the prior close. This broke a swing low thirteen sessions old, past the 5 a 2B needs, and took it back the same session. That's the fastest kind of reclaim. MKSI did this on 2025-11-21 and closed the day at 144.00.
questions.lesson_line: Name it by the low it broke. An old swing low is a 2B.

wrong.An Oops, reclaimed the same day: Same-day isn't the test. An Oops is judged on yesterday's low, and this low is thirteen sessions old.
wrong.A Remount, it retook an old low: A Remount needs five or more closes under the line. This had none.
wrong.A breakdown, it broke a low: It closed back above the same day. A breakdown stays under.

questions.simple: A 2B. The low it broke was thirteen sessions old, not yesterday's, so it's not an Oops.

deeper.trap: Don't name it by the dip alone. An Oops is judged on yesterday's low. This broke a swing low thirteen sessions old, so it's a 2B.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed look-alike tell (Oops)

questions.q: Dip under, close back over. Which setup are you trading?
choices: A U&R, the level is an average
A 2B, it reclaimed the line
An Oops, it dipped and recovered
A Remount, it retook the average
questions.story: A leader dips under its rising 50-day and closes back above it the same day. There's no swing low anywhere near it.
questions.answer: A U&R, the level is an average
questions.why: A U&R, an undercut and rally. The level is what names it. A 2B needs an old swing low. A rising 20 EMA or 50-day makes it a U&R. So does a prior high, a round number or the 10-session range low. Same move, different level, different setup. Name the level first, then the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Name the level. A swing low is a 2B. A rising average is a U&R.

wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed the line: A 2B breaks an old swing low. A moving average makes it a U&R.
wrong.An Oops, it dipped and recovered: An Oops breaks yesterday's low and takes back the prior close. This was an average.
wrong.A Remount, it retook the average: A Remount comes after five or more closes under the line. This closed back above the same day.

questions.simple: A U&R. The level was a rising average, and a 2B needs an old swing low.

deeper.trap: Name the level before the label. A rising 20 EMA or 50-day, a prior high, a round number or the 10-session range low makes it a U&R. A swing low at least 5 sessions old makes it a 2B. The dip and the reclaim look the same, so the level is the tell.

reasons: +2 the level test is the card's tb.level criterion, still held (D-101)
+1 rests on one card line

questions.q: Six closes under, then back above. What setup is that?
choices: A Remount, bought on the retake
A 2B, it reclaimed the broken low
An Oops, it reclaimed the prior close
A spring, it retook the floor
questions.story: Last bar: the sixth close in a row under an old swing low. Tomorrow it trades back above it.
questions.answer: A Remount, bought on the retake
questions.why: A Remount. A 2B gets back above the broken low fast, inside about 3 sessions. Six closes under is way too long. By then the sellers who broke it have been right for more than a week. That's a breakdown that came back, not a failed break. Five or more closes under, then a retake, is a Remount. It's bought on the retake of the line, with its own rules. GS had 6 closes under its 236.64 low in January 2017.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. Five or more is a Remount.

wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed the broken low: A 2B gets back above fast. Six closes under is too long.
wrong.An Oops, it reclaimed the prior close: An Oops takes back the prior close the same day, off yesterday's low. This stayed under for six closes.
wrong.A spring, it retook the floor: A spring closes back inside the same day or the next. This stayed under for six closes.

questions.simple: A Remount. Six closes under is too many for a 2B, which gets back above fast.

deeper.trap: Count the closes under the line. Five or more, then a retake, is a Remount, bought on the retake of the line. It's not the reclaim of a low.

reasons: +2 the reclaim-window grading is held (D-102)
+1 rests on one dossier example

questions.q: 2B or a spring?
choices: A spring, the level is a floor
A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low
An Oops, it closed back inside
A Remount, it retook the floor
questions.story: A stock has traded sideways for 20 sessions and touched its floor three times. It dips under the floor and closes back inside the same day.
questions.answer: A spring, the level is a floor
questions.why: A spring. A spring's level is the floor of a sideways range of 15 sessions or more, touched at least twice, with the close back inside the same day or the next. This stock traded sideways for 20 sessions and touched its floor three times. A 2B breaks a single swing low.
questions.lesson_line: A range floor is a spring. A single swing low is a 2B.

wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low: A 2B's level is a single swing low, not the floor of a range.
wrong.An Oops, it closed back inside: An Oops is judged on yesterday's low.
wrong.A Remount, it retook the floor: A Remount follows five or more closes under the level. This closed back inside the same day.

questions.simple: A spring. The level is the floor of a long sideways range, not a single swing low.

deeper.trap: A spring and a 2B look alike on a chart, so the level tells them apart. A spring's level is the floor of a sideways range of 15 sessions or more, touched at least twice. A 2B breaks a single swing low.

reasons: +2 the level test is the card's tb.level criterion, still held (D-101)
+1 rests on one card line

questions.q: Is it a 2B?
choices: No, no prior swing low to break
Yes, it dipped under and reclaimed
Yes, it is a Remount of the low
No, it needs a gap down first
questions.story: A stock falls for six days in a row. Today it dips under yesterday's low and closes a little higher.
questions.answer: No, no prior swing low to break
questions.why: No. A one-day dip under yesterday's low is an Oops, not a 2B: the level must be at least 5 sessions old. In a six-day decline each low is only a day old, so there is no prior swing low to break. Calling any dip under yesterday's low a 2B is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Calling any dip under yesterday's low a 2B is a mistake.

wrong.Yes, it dipped under and reclaimed: A dip under yesterday's low is not a 2B.
wrong.Yes, it is a Remount of the low: A Remount follows five or more closes under a level.
wrong.No, it needs a gap down first: The open does not decide it. The level does: a 2B breaks a swing low at least 5 sessions old.

questions.simple: No. Yesterday's low is only one day old, and a 2B needs a swing low at least 5 sessions old.

questions.q: Second trip under, second reclaim. Can you buy it as a 2B?

Yes, it reclaimed the low
Yes, a second try looks stronger
No, the reclaim came too fast

questions.answer: No, it's not the first break

Monday's dip went 3.9% under, deeper than I like anyway. A second break tells you the low didn't scare the sellers off the first time. That's a weaker picture, not a better one.
questions.lesson_line: Only the first break of the low counts.

wrong.Yes, a second try looks stronger: It's weaker. The low already gave way once.
wrong.No, the reclaim came too fast: Right call, wrong reason. Fast is good. It's the second break.

questions.simple: No. Only the first break of the low counts, and Friday already used it.

deeper.trap: A second try can feel stronger, but only the first break counts. The break has to be the first session to trade under that low since it formed.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed first-break criterion

wrong.The swing low was too recent: It was an old swing low, well past 5 sessions.
wrong.It was slow to close back above: It came back fast. That part's fine.
